lessons.title: Weeds, invader plants and the law
lessons.html:
Defining the problem

A weed is any plant growing where it is not wanted, competing with crops or pasture, contaminating harvested grain or creating hazards on roadsides and industrial sites. An invasive alien plant is a species from another country that spreads aggressively into natural areas, displacing indigenous vegetation. In South Africa invasive plants use large volumes of water, increase fire intensity, reduce grazing capacity and threaten biodiversity.

Common examples

TypeExamples
Crop weedsBlackjack, thorn apple (stinkblaar), nutgrass, pigweed
Invasive treesBlack wattle, Port Jackson, rooikrans, pines, gums along watercourses, mesquite in arid areas
Invasive shrubs and herbsLantana, bugweed, triffid weed (Chromolaena), famine weed (Parthenium), pompom weed
Succulents and aquatic plantsPrickly pear, water hyacinth

Legal framework

  • National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004 (NEMBA): its Alien and Invasive Species Regulations and lists place species in categories. In broad terms, Category 1a species must be combated and eradicated; Category 1b species must be controlled and contained; Category 2 species need a permit for specified areas or uses; Category 3 species may not be further planted or traded and are treated more strictly in riparian areas. Landowners have obligations to control listed species on their land. Always check the current list for a specific species.
  • Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 (CARA): also addresses weeds and invader plants on farmland as part of protecting natural agricultural resources.
  • Act 36 of 1947: herbicides must be registered and used according to the label, and operators applying them for reward must be registered.
  • National Water Act 36 of 1998: work near watercourses must avoid pollution.

Government programmes, such as the Working for Water programme, have cleared large areas of invasive plants, often with community teams, and contractors working on such projects must follow programme standards.

lessons.title: Control methods and herbicide principles
lessons.html:
Integrated weed management

No single method controls weeds and invaders long term. Combine methods to suit the species, density, site and budget.

Methods

  • Prevention: clean seed, clean machinery between fields, control weeds before they seed, avoid moving contaminated soil or sand.
  • Mechanical: hand pulling of seedlings, hoeing, slashing, felling, ring-barking and uprooting. Many woody invaders, such as wattles and gums, coppice (resprout) from stumps unless the stump is treated.
  • Cultural: crop rotation, competitive crops, correct grazing management, mulching, and restoring vigorous indigenous cover.
  • Biological: host-specific insects, mites or pathogens released under official programmes, for example agents used against prickly pear and some wattles. Biocontrol reduces vigour or seed production over time; avoid destroying biocontrol populations with careless herbicide use.
  • Chemical: registered herbicides applied by suitable techniques.

Herbicide types

CharacteristicMeaning
SelectiveControls certain plants, such as broadleaf weeds in grass, without killing others
Non-selectiveDamages most plants it contacts
ContactKills the parts it touches; fast but roots may survive
SystemicMoves within the plant to roots and growing points; needed for perennials
Pre-emergenceApplied to soil to stop seedlings establishing
Post-emergenceApplied to growing plants

Herbicides are grouped by mode of action. Repeated use of one group selects resistant weeds; rotate or mix modes of action as labels allow.

Application techniques for invaders

  • Foliar spray for seedlings, shrubs and regrowth.
  • Cut stump: fell the plant and apply herbicide to the freshly cut stump immediately.
  • Basal stem: apply to the lower stem bark of thin-barked plants.
  • Frill or stem injection: cut into the bark of standing trees and apply herbicide to the cuts.

Use only techniques and rates on the label of a product registered for that species and situation, and add dye where allowed so treated plants are visible.

lessons.title: Planning, follow-up and safe practice
lessons.html:
Planning a clearing programme

  1. Survey and map infestations by species, density and age, noting watercourses, sensitive areas and access.
  2. Prioritise: start with lightly infested areas and outlying populations to stop spread, protect high-value areas such as riparian zones, and target Category 1a species.
  3. Select methods for each species and density.
  4. Plan follow-up: seed banks can remain viable in the soil for many years. Initial clearing without follow-up is wasted money.
  5. Plan rehabilitation: re-establish indigenous vegetation or pasture to compete with seedlings and protect soil from erosion.
  6. Budget and resource teams, equipment, herbicides and supervision across several seasons.

Timing

Systemic herbicides work best on actively growing plants. Treat before seed set. Follow-up treatments of seedlings are cheapest when plants are small. Timing differs between summer and winter rainfall regions.

Working near water

Riparian zones are often heavily invaded. Use only products registered for use near water, protect water from spray drift and spills, mix away from the watercourse, and never wash equipment in streams.

Safety

  • Chainsaw and brushcutter work requires trained operators with chaps, helmet, visor, hearing protection and boots.
  • Plan felling direction and keep a safe distance between workers.
  • Wear chemical PPE when mixing and applying herbicides, as the label specifies.
  • Do not spray in wind conditions that cause drift onto crops, gardens or water.
  • Have first aid kits and emergency transport on site; remote clearing sites can be far from help. Hands-on first aid training by an accredited provider is required.
  • Be aware of snakes, bees and heat stress in dense vegetation.

Monitoring and records

Record areas treated, species, methods, products and quantities, dates and teams. Photograph fixed points before and after. Revisit to measure kill rate and regrowth and to schedule follow-ups.

Key points

  • Invasive alien plants use water, increase fire risk and displace indigenous vegetation.
  • NEMBA 10 of 2004 categories determine landowner obligations; check the current list for each species.
  • Combine prevention, mechanical, cultural, biological and chemical methods.
  • Use systemic herbicides and correct techniques such as cut stump treatment to prevent resprouting.
  • Plan follow-up and rehabilitation for several seasons, and protect water and workers.

options.text: National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004

options.text: To prevent the stumps from resprouting
